codex: The Amazon's staple root. Sweet varieties carry under 50 mg/kg cyanide — peeling and thorough cooking clears it. Feeds half the tropics for a reason.
description: tall stalks with hand-shaped leaves and thick pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Manioc. Tall stalks, hand-shaped leaves, thick roots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: roots (the food — peel first), young leaves (cooked greens only, never raw). Rot fast after harvest.
knowledgeLevels.3: Sweet varieties: peel + cook through and they're safe. Bitter varieties can carry 400 mg/kg cyanide and need days of work — grate, ferment 2-3 days, press out the juice, roast into farinha. Cooking alone does NOT clear bitter roots (boiling removes only 10-75%).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: bitter roots yield more starch and make the best farinha — if you do the full detox. Sweet for quick meals, bitter for the pantry. Harvest only what you'll process within days.

lookalikeNote: Sweet and bitter varieties look IDENTICAL — same palmate leaves, same roots. The only safe test is knowledge: know the field it came from, or the person who planted it. If you don't know which it is, treat it as bitter.
name: Sweet Manioc
preparation: Peel completely (toxins concentrate in the peel), then boil, roast, or fry until fully cooked through. Never eat raw. Roots rot within days of harvest — cook or process fast.
sources: FAO CXC 73-2013 (Codex code of practice for cassava processing)

uses.note: roots peeled and cooked; young leaves boiled
farinha (toasted flour) from fully detoxed roots

codex: The dangerous twin. Bitter manioc feeds millions — but only because the processing is a ritual nobody skips. Grate, ferment, press, roast. In that order, every time.
description: tall stalks with hand-shaped leaves and thick pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Manioc. Looks exactly like the sweet kind. That is the problem.
knowledgeLevels.2: The cyanide lives in linamarin, locked in the root. Grating ruptures the cells so the enzyme linamarase can break it down — that's why you grate BEFORE fermenting.
knowledgeLevels.3: The full rite: peel, grate, ferment the mash 2-3 days (never less), press out every drop of juice, roast dry. Fermenting less than 2 days leaves dangerous cyanide in the flour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the poison is the point — bitter varieties out-yield sweet and their farinha keeps for months. Sulfur-rich foods (meat, eggs) help your body clear small doses. Never let the desperate eat it half-processed.

lookalikeNote: Indistinguishable from sweet manioc by sight — same leaves, same roots. Bitter roots can carry up to 400 mg HCN per kg (8x sweet). This is the one that kills when hunger makes people shortcut the work.
name: Bitter Manioc
preparation: Cooking alone is NOT enough — boiling removes only 10-75% of the cyanide. Full detox: peel, grate to rupture the tissue, ferment the mash 2-3 days, press out ALL the juice, then roast dry into farinha or gari. Skip a step and it can kill (~200 deaths a year worldwide).
sources: FAO CXC 73-2013 (Codex code of practice for cassava processing)

uses.note: only after the full grate-ferment-press-roast detox
tucupi (the pressed juice) is lethal raw, a delicacy after days of boiling

codex: The floodplain palm. Fatty purple pulp, eaten by the bowlful with farinha. Açaí feeds the river towns — and climbing the palm is the price.
description: a slender palm with a crown of arching fronds and hanging clusters of dark purple berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Açaí. Dark berries on a tall thin palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (mash for pulp). The trunk's heart (palmito) is food too — but cutting it kills the palm.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is fatty and filling, a real meal with farinha. Spoils in a day — eat it fresh or not at all.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: multi-stemmed clumps regrow after cutting — harvest palmito from the suckers, never the mother stem. Best pulp comes from berries soaked warm, not hot.

lookalikeNote: Bacaba and patauá are close cousins with similar berries — all three are safe. The dangerous lookalike is none: learn the palm, not the berry.
name: Açaí
preparation: Soak the berries in warm water, then mash and strain — the thick purple pulp is the food. Eat fresh; it ferments within a day.

uses.note: heart of palm from sucker stems (sustainable cut)

codex: The forest's savings account. One pod holds a dozen nuts, each one pure fat and protein. The trees only fruit in old-growth — no plantation has ever matched the wild.
description: a giant emergent tree dropping heavy cannonball pods the size of a head

knowledgeLevels.1: Brazil nut. Huge tree, huge pods, rich nuts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: nuts (eat). The pod is a wooden cannonball — crack it, don't bite it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: among the most calorie-dense wild foods on earth. A handful is a meal. Keep dry and they last months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: agoutis bury the nuts and forget some — that's how the tree plants itself. Watch where agoutis feed and you'll find the mother trees.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else drops pods like cannonballs. The agouti is the only animal strong-toothed enough to open them — follow the agouti.
name: Brazil Nuts
preparation: Crack the woody pod (machete, rock, or patience), extract the nuts, eat raw or roasted. Don't stand under the tree in pod season.
sources: FAO non-wood forest products: Brazil nut

uses.note: nuts raw or roasted, in the shell they keep for months

codex: Not a tree — the world's biggest herb. An old roça always has banana: the first thing planted, the last thing to die.
description: a giant herb with huge paddle leaves and hanging hands of curved yellow-green fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Banana. Peel, eat.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (ripe raw, green cooked), flower bud (cooked), stalk core (cooked).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: instant energy, potassium. The leaves wrap food for roasting and thatch a roof.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the 'tree' dies after fruiting — the suckers at its base are the next crop. Cut the old stem to feed the young.

lookalikeNote: Plantains look identical on the plant — they're starchier and must be cooked. Taste a corner: sweet means banana, bland means plantain.
name: Banana
preparation: Peel and eat ripe. Green ones cook like a vegetable. The flower bud and inner stalk are cooked greens.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; green fruit cooked
flower bud and stalk core, cooked

codex: The smell gives it away before your eyes do — chocolate and pineapple at once. The pulp is dessert; the seeds are chocolate waiting to happen.
description: a small tree with huge brown fuzzy pods hanging from the trunk, smelling of chocolate and pineapple

knowledgeLevels.1: Cupuaçu. Big brown pod, incredible smell, tangy cream inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat raw), seeds (dry and grind for cupulate chocolate).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is rich and filling — juice it, or eat it straight. High in fats that feed you fast.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits drop when ripe — gather from the ground, don't pick. The pulp ferments fast; eat or juice within a day.

lookalikeNote: Cacao's big cousin — both fruit straight from the trunk (cauliflory). Cupuaçu pods are bigger, brown and fuzzy; cacao pods are smaller, ribbed, yellow-red.
name: Cupuaçu
preparation: Crack the pod, scoop the creamy pulp raw. Seeds can be dried and ground like cacao — that's cupulate, the Amazon's chocolate.

uses.note: seeds dried and ground as chocolate (cupulate)

codex: Chocolate grows on trees here — almost. The pulp is the treat; the seeds are a week of work away from chocolate.
description: an understory tree with ribbed yellow-red pods growing straight out of the trunk

knowledgeLevels.1: Cacao. Sweet pulp around bitter seeds, straight off the trunk.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat fresh), seeds (ferment, dry, roast for chocolate).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pulp is quick sugar and water. The seeds are fat and calories — but only after fermenting 3-5 days and drying.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: unfermented seeds are just bitter. The fermentation is the whole trick — heap them in leaves, turn daily, then dry in the sun.

lookalikeNote: Cupuaçu's smaller cousin — same trunk-fruiting habit. Cacao pods are ribbed and colorful; cupuaçu pods are brown and fuzzy.
name: Cacao
preparation: Split the pod and suck the sweet-tart pulp off the seeds — eat it fresh. The seeds themselves are bitter raw; they need fermenting and drying to become chocolate.

uses.note: pulp sucked fresh off the seeds

codex: The Amazon's breadfruit — starchy, nutty, filling. And the one palm you can harvest the heart from guilt-free: it suckers, so the clump lives on.
description: a clustering spiny palm hung with bunches of orange-red plum-sized fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Pupunha. Orange fruit clusters on a spiny palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (boiled), heart of palm (the sustainable one — cut one stem, the clump regrows).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the boiled fruit eats like a chestnut crossed with squash — real starch, real meal.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: watch for the weevil grubs in fallen fruit — the locals eat those too. Cut heart-of-palm only from multi-stem clumps.

lookalikeNote: The spiny trunk is the ID — rings of black spines. Tucumã is spiny too but its fruit is smaller and oilier.
name: Pupunha (Peach Palm)
preparation: Boil the fruit in salted water 30-60 minutes until the flesh softens — eating it raw is gritty and unpleasant. Split, remove the seed, eat the starchy flesh.

uses.note: heart of palm from sucker stems

codex: The weed-tree that feeds everyone. Guava colonizes every clearing — where people were, guava still is.
description: a shrubby tree with smooth peeling bark and round yellow-green fragrant fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Guava. Fragrant, soft, pink inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat whole). Leaves make a tea for gut trouble.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: vitamin C by the handful. The leaf tea is a real antidiarrheal — worth knowing.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: guava marks old habitation — a guava thicket means a roça was here, and roças mean manioc gone wild nearby.

lookalikeNote: The peeling bark is the giveaway — smooth, mottled, like sunburn peeling. Nothing poisonous in the Amazon looks like this.
name: Guava
preparation: Eat ripe and soft, skin and all. Hard green ones need ripening off the tree — or cooking.

codex: Born in South America, raised by the whole tropics. The crown you twist off is the next plant — stick it in the ground.
description: a spiky rosette of sword leaves with a single golden cone of a fruit rising from the center

knowledgeLevels.1: Pineapple. Spiky outside, gold inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat ripe). The crown replants.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sugar, water, and bromelain — the enzyme that tenderizes meat and burns your tongue if you overdo it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: plant the crowns in a row and you have a living fence that fruits. Unripe juice tenderizes tough meat in an hour.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else makes this fruit. Unripe it is all acid — the mouth-burn is the warning, not poison.
name: Pineapple
preparation: Twist off the crown, slice away the spiky skin, eat. Unripe pineapple burns the mouth — wait for gold and fragrance.

codex: The vine that smells like the tropics are supposed to. Tart, fragrant, and the juice knocks you pleasantly sideways at dusk.
description: a climbing vine with alien-looking purple-and-white flowers and wrinkled purple-yellow fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Maracujá. Wrinkled fruit, incredible smell, scoop the inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp with seeds (eat). The wrinkled ones are the sweet ones.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the juice is mildly sedative — the old-timers drink it at night for sleep.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the vine fruits heaviest on forest edges where it climbs into the light. Follow the smell in fruiting season.

lookalikeNote: Many passionflower vines are ornamental with inedible fruit. Edulis has the wrinkled purple fruit and three-lobed leaves — when in doubt, smell: ripe maracujá is unmistakable.
name: Maracujá (Passion Fruit)
preparation: Cut and scoop the aromatic pulp — seeds and all. Wrinkled skin means ripe and sweet.

codex: The vitamin bomb. Sixty times the vitamin C of an orange — the floodplain's answer to scurvy, if you can stand the sour.
description: a bushy riverside shrub with small round red-purple fruit, standing in the floodwater half the year

knowledgeLevels.1: Camu-camu. Sour little riverbank fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat fresh, juice it).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the richest natural vitamin C source known. Eat a handful a week and scurvy can't touch you.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it fruits as the waters rise — the flood brings the medicine. Pulp freezes and dries well for the dry months.

lookalikeNote: Grows where the river stands — the flood tolerance is the ID. Small myrtle-family fruit, nothing toxic mimics it here.
name: Camu-camu
preparation: Eat the tart fruit fresh or squeeze for juice — staggeringly sour, staggeringly full of vitamin C. A spoonful of pulp covers days of need.

codex: The custard apple of the Amazon. Fragile, perfumed, and gone in a day — eat it standing under the tree.
description: a small tree with spiny green heart-shaped fruit that turns yellow and perfumed when ripe

knowledgeLevels.1: Soursop. Spiny green fruit, white creamy inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat — SPIT OUT the seeds). Leaves make a strong tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is rich and filling. The seeds carry annonacin — swallow one whole and you're fine; chew them and you're not.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: don't make soursop a daily staple — heavy long-term use of the pulp and leaf tea is linked to nerve trouble. A treat, not a diet.

lookalikeNote: Biriba is the lookalike — same family, softer spines, smaller fruit. Both are safe; both hide seeds you shouldn't chew.
name: Soursop
preparation: Open ripe fruit and eat the pulp, spitting out the large black seeds — they are toxic (annonacin). Never chew or grind the seeds.

uses.note: pulp raw, seeds spat out whole

codex: Soursop's gentler cousin. Custard in a spiny jacket — the Amazon's ice cream before freezers.
description: a small tree with yellow heart-shaped fruit covered in soft fleshy spines

knowledgeLevels.1: Biriba. Yellow spiny fruit, custard inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat). Skin and seeds are not food.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet, soft, fast energy. Ripe means yellow and fragrant — green means wait.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits bruise if you look at them wrong. Eat under the tree; carry pulp, not fruit.

lookalikeNote: Soursop's lookalike — smaller, yellower, softer spines. Safe either way, so the confusion costs you nothing but a name.
name: Biriba
preparation: Eat fully ripe (yellow, fragrant) — scoop the custard pulp. Unripe fruit is bland and chalky.

codex: Patience fruit. Pick it yellow or pick it twice — the unripe latex will glue your mouth shut and you'll deserve it.
description: a tall tree with round yellow fruit that drips sticky white latex when unripe

knowledgeLevels.1: Abiu. Round yellow fruit, sweet jelly inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat when fully ripe). Unripe fruit is full of sticky latex — avoid.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: translucent sweet pulp, eaten with a spoon. Good quick calories.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: grease your lips before eating — even ripe fruit leaks a little latex. Fully tree-ripened is the only kind worth picking.

lookalikeNote: Unripe abiu looks ready but isn't — the latex is the test. If white sap beads from the stem, walk away and come back in a week.
name: Abiu
preparation: Eat only fully ripe (deep yellow, slightly soft) — scoop the translucent pulp. Unripe fruit's latex sticks lips together painfully.

codex: The spiny one. Tucumã doesn't want to be picked — the trunk is armored. The orange pulp is worth the negotiation.
description: a tall spiny palm with dense bunches of small orange oily fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Tucumã. Orange palm fruit, spiny trunk — approach carefully.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat), seed (hard, not food). The spines are the tax.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: oily, vitamin-A-rich pulp. Real food, and the fiber from the leaves makes hammocks.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut the whole bunch with a long pole — never climb a spiny palm. Fallen fruit ferments fast; gather daily.

lookalikeNote: Spiny trunk + small orange fruit = tucumã. Murumuru is spiny too but shorter, with bigger fruit. Both are safe.
name: Tucumã
preparation: Eat the oily orange pulp fresh off the seed. The trunk spines are vicious — harvest bunches with a pole, never by climbing.

codex: Açaí's quiet cousin. The bacaba wine — purple, oily, faintly sweet — is what the river towns drink when açaí runs thin.
description: a tall slender palm with hanging clusters of dark purple oily berries, thinner than açaí

knowledgeLevels.1: Bacaba. Dark berries like açaí, oilier.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (mash for drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the 'wine' is thinner and oilier than açaí — an acquired taste that grows on you fast when hungry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits when açaí doesn't — the two palms stagger their seasons. Learn both and the river never runs dry of purple.

lookalikeNote: Açaí vs bacaba: açaí berries are rounder and the palm clumps; bacaba is single-stemmed and taller. Both safe — the confusion is harmless.
name: Bacaba
preparation: Soak berries warm, mash and strain like açaí — the result is an oily purple drink. Eat fresh.

codex: The olive tree of the Amazon. The fruit is nearly half oil — press it and you have cooking fat that doesn't spoil.
description: a very tall palm with long clusters of green-purple fruit that feels greasy to the touch

knowledgeLevels.1: Patauá. Tall palm, greasy-feeling fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit pulp (eat, press for oil).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the oil is the prize — cooking fat that keeps without refrigeration. The pulp itself is rich and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: mash the pulp in warm water and the oil floats — skim it. A bottle of patauá oil is trade wealth.

lookalikeNote: Bacaba's taller, greasier cousin — same genus. The oily feel of the fruit is the ID. Both safe.
name: Patauá
preparation: Eat the pulp fresh, or mash in warm water and skim the oil that rises — excellent cooking oil that keeps.

uses.note: pulp fresh or pressed for oil

codex: The palm that feeds the beetles that feed you. Inajá fruit falls, the weevils come, and the grubs are the real harvest.
description: a stout palm with a swollen trunk base and large bunches of yellow-orange plum-like fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Inajá. Yellow fruit bunches on a fat-based palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat). Fallen fruit draws palm weevils.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet oily pulp. The fallen fruit is bait — come back in a week for the grubs, which are pure fat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the weevil grubs are the higher-value crop. Manage an inajá grove like a grub farm and you'll never lack fat.

lookalikeNote: The swollen trunk base is distinctive. The fruit resembles small plums; nothing toxic shares the shape and the palm.
name: Inajá
preparation: Eat the ripe yellow-orange pulp fresh. Leave fallen fruit as weevil bait — harvest the grubs days later.

uses.note: palm weevil grubs from fallen fruit

codex: Butter that grows on a spiny palm. The seed is half fat — the cosmetics industry pays fortunes for it; you'll eat it.
description: a short viciously spiny palm with bunches of yellow-brown fruit like small coconuts

knowledgeLevels.1: Murumuru. Spiny palm, coconut-like fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat), seed (crack for the fatty kernel).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the kernel is nearly half butter — dense calories. The pulp is sweet and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spines are the whole problem and the whole defense. Harvest with a pole; the seeds keep for months in the shell.

lookalikeNote: Tucumã's shorter, meaner cousin — both spiny, both safe. Murumuru fruit is bigger and the palm stays short.
name: Murumuru
preparation: Eat the pulp fresh; crack the hard seed for the fatty kernel — eat raw or render into butter.

codex: Delicious and armed. The pulp is superb — and the seed wears a coat of tiny wooden daggers that will ruin your mouth if you bite.
description: a tall tree with green-orange fruit the size of an orange, hiding a spiny pit inside

knowledgeLevels.1: Piquiarana. Tasty fruit, dangerous pit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat). The pit is armored — never bite it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich oily pulp, excellent calories. The spines on the endocarp are the whole lesson.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: scrape the pulp off with your teeth like the locals — never close your jaw on the pit. The seed inside is edible too, once you get past the armor.

lookalikeNote: No poisonous lookalike — the danger is built in. The thin woody spines covering the pit stick into lips and gums of the careless.
name: Piquiarana
preparation: Eat the oily pulp by scraping it off the pit with your teeth — NEVER bite through. The pit's endocarp is covered in thin sharp spines.

uses.note: pulp scraped from the spiny pit

codex: Two foods, one tree, and a poison in between. The apple is juice; the nut is a chemistry lesson you do not skip.
description: a spreading tree with pear-shaped juicy fruit, each one carrying a kidney-shaped nut underneath

knowledgeLevels.1: Cashew. Juicy apple on top, weird nut hanging below.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the apple (eat fresh, juice it). The nut is POISON until roasted.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the apple is sweet, astringent, and ferments in a day — juice it fast. The nut's shell holds caustic cardol oil, kin to poison ivy.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: roast the nuts IN the shell first — the heat destroys the cardol — then crack. Never handle raw shell oil with bare hands; it blisters.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else grows its nut outside the fruit. The apple is unmistakable — but the nut it carries is the trap.
name: Cashew
preparation: Eat the apple fresh or juiced within a day (it ferments fast). The nut MUST be roasted in its shell before cracking — the shell oil (cardol/urushiol) burns skin and mouth raw.
sources: The Old Foodie: The Cashew Nut

uses.note: nut only after roasting in shell

codex: The giant's pantry. The lily's seeds feed you, its stalks feed you — the whole plant is a meal wearing a flower.
description: enormous round floating leaves with upturned rims, some wide enough to hold a child

knowledgeLevels.1: Giant water lily. Huge floating leaves, night-blooming flowers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds (dry and roast), stalks and rhizomes (cooked like vegetables).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the seeds dry and roast into a starchy snack, or grind into flour. The stalks cook like greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather the seed pods as the flowers fade. Sun-dry thoroughly — damp seeds rot, dry seeds keep for months.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else on the water is this size. The leaf undersides carry sharp spines — handle pads by the rim, not from below.
name: Giant Water Lily
preparation: Collect the seeds, sun-dry, then roast — they pop and puff into a starchy snack, or grind to flour. Cook stalks and rhizomes as vegetables.

uses.note: seeds dried and roasted, or ground to flour

codex: The Amazon's own yam — not the African import. White-fleshed, delicate, and it climbs the trees if you let it.
description: a climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and knobby white tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Cush-cush yam. Climbing vine, white tubers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (cook). The vine dies back in the dry — mark the spot.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: starchy staple, mild and filling. Digs easier in the wet season when the ground is soft.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: replant the tuber tips and vine cuttings — a yam patch is a savings account that compounds.

lookalikeNote: Taro grows nearby in the wet spots — taro has arrowhead leaves on stalks from the base; yam climbs. Cook both thoroughly.
name: Cush-cush Yam
preparation: Dig the tubers, peel, and cook thoroughly — boil or roast until soft all the way through. Never eat raw.

codex: The floodplain's potato. Taro loves standing water — and it will punish you with a mouthful of needles if you get impatient.
description: big arrowhead leaves on long stalks rising from muddy water, with starchy corms below

knowledgeLevels.1: Taro. Big leaves in the mud, starchy corms underneath.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: corms and young leaves — BOTH must be cooked. Raw taro is full of calcium oxalate needles.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the corm is dense staple starch. The itch in your throat means you undercooked it — boil longer, change the water.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: taro is the flood-season crop — it thrives where manioc drowns. Plant the corm tops in the receding flood and eat while others go hungry.

lookalikeNote: Wild elephant-ear relatives share the leaf shape and are far more irritating — only eat taro you planted or that a local confirms. The rule is absolute: cook it like you mean it.
name: Taro
preparation: Peel and boil the corms thoroughly (change the water once) — raw taro's oxalate crystals burn the mouth and throat. Young leaves need long boiling too.

uses.note: corms peeled, boiled well; young leaves boiled long

codex: Born in the Americas, feeding the world. The roça's easy child — plant a vine cutting, come back to dinner.
description: a sprawling vine with heart-shaped leaves and sweet orange-fleshed tubers

knowledgeLevels.1: Sweet potato. Vine, orange tubers, sweet.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (raw is fine, cooked is better), young leaves (cooked greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fast energy, vitamin A in the orange flesh. The leaves are decent greens — boil them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the easiest crop in the Amazon — vine cuttings root in days. A roça of sweet potato is a month from planting to eating.

lookalikeNote: Ornamental morning-glory vines share the flower shape but not the tuber. Dig first, admire flowers later.
name: Sweet Potato
preparation: Eat raw if you must; roast or boil for the real meal. Young leaves are cooked greens.

uses.note: tubers raw or cooked; leaves as cooked greens

codex: The fast one. Papaya goes from seed to fruit in a year — the pioneer's fruit, first to colonize every clearing.
description: a soft-trunked small tree with a crown of huge lobed leaves and melon-like fruit hanging below

knowledgeLevels.1: Papaya. Soft trunk, big lobed leaves, melon fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit (eat). Unripe fruit has latex — cooks use it to tenderize meat.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: gentle on the stomach, good when you're recovering. The seeds are peppery — a few are fine, a handful is a purge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: papaya marks fresh disturbance — it fruits within a year of a clearing. Follow the papaya to find where people were, recently.

lookalikeNote: Ripe is the rule — green papaya's latex irritates. Wait for yellow-orange skin and a sweet smell.
name: Papaya
preparation: Eat fully ripe (yellow-orange, fragrant) — scoop the flesh, spit or swallow the peppery seeds sparingly.

codex: The tree that shoots back. Assacu doesn't want to be eaten, climbed, burned, or stood under — respect all four.
description: a huge tree with a trunk studded in conical thorns and pumpkin-shaped pods that explode

knowledgeLevels.1: Assacu. Thorny trunk, exploding pods. Stay back.
knowledgeLevels.2: The pods burst at 240 km/h, firing seeds like shrapnel. The white latex blisters skin and blinds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for eating — ever. The latex was dart poison. The wood makes canoes, if you dare fell it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn this tree the way you learn a cliff edge — by location, not by touch. Never shelter under one in the dry season, never burn its wood (the smoke bites).

lookalikeNote: The conical thorns are unmistakable — 'monkey-no-climb'. Nothing edible in the Amazon wears armor like this. If the trunk has thorns and the pods are pumpkin-shaped, walk away.
name: Assacu (Sandbox Tree)
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Seeds and latex are violently toxic — purgative at best, poisoning at worst. Don't climb (thorns), don't stand under ripe pods (explosive seeds at 150+ mph), don't get the latex in your eyes.
sources: Google Arts & Culture: Curiously Dangerous — The Sandbox Tree

codex: The pretty weed that kills. Mottled seeds like engraved beans — beautiful, and a few will stop your heart. The oil is safe; the seed is not.
description: a tall weed with star-shaped leaves and spiny pods holding beautiful mottled beans

knowledgeLevels.1: Castor bean. Star leaves, spiny pods, pretty mottled seeds.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds hold ricin — one of the most potent plant poisons known. A handful can kill an adult.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none raw. The pressed oil (properly processed) is safe — the poison stays in the mash, not the oil.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it colonizes every disturbed patch in the tropics. Learn it young, because it WILL grow by your camp.

lookalikeNote: The star-shaped leaves and mottled seeds are distinctive. It grows exactly where you'd camp — clearings, riverbanks, ruins. Check the ground before you let anyone forage casually.
name: Castor Bean
preparation: DO NOT EAT the seeds — they contain ricin; even a few chewed seeds can be fatal. Only properly heat-processed castor oil is safe.

codex: The emergent giant's seeds are oil and protein — and chemistry that doesn't belong in a stomach. The fiber built life jackets; the seeds build nothing edible.
description: a towering emergent tree with a buttressed trunk, dropping pods full of silky fiber and dark seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Kapok. Giant tree, silky pods, dark seeds.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds carry cyclopropenoid fatty acids (malvalic, sterculic) — the oil is classed non-edible, good for soap and biodiesel, not for you.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the fiber is the treasure — buoyant, water-resistant, warm. Stuff pillows, insulate, caulk canoes.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: kapok emergents are landmarks and spirit-houses across the Amazon. Harvest the fallen fiber; leave the seeds.

lookalikeNote: The buttressed trunk and emergent crown are the ID. Don't confuse the seeds with any edible nut — the fiber gives them away.
name: Kapok Seeds
preparation: DO NOT EAT. The seeds contain cyclopropenoid fatty acids; the oil is treated as non-edible (used for biodiesel and soap). Harvest the silky fiber instead — superb insulation and stuffing.
sources: MDPI Plants: The Biology of the Genus Ceiba (2022 review)
ResearchGate: Chemical Composition of Kapok Seed

uses.note: silky fiber for insulation, stuffing, caulking

codex: Rubber built Manaus and Belém — and the seeds built nothing but trouble raw. Cyanide in a shell, dinner after a long boil.
description: a tall plantation tree with three-part leaves and three-lobed pods that explode, flinging large mottled seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Rubber tree. Three-leaflet leaves, exploding pods.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds carry linamarin — cyanogenic, ~186 mg/kg. Raw, they're poison. Locals eat them only after thorough, long cooking.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: famine food at best. The latex is the real crop — tap it, don't eat it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the pods explode like the assacu's smaller cousins — gather seeds from the ground, and boil them like you mean it, twice.

lookalikeNote: The three-lobed exploding pods are shared with its cousins. Don't confuse the seeds with Brazil nuts — rubber seeds are mottled, flatter, and raw-poisonous.
name: Rubber Seeds
preparation: POISONOUS RAW (cyanogenic glycosides). Only edible after thorough prolonged cooking — the way riverside communities prepare them. When in doubt, leave them; this is famine food, not a snack.
sources: Universiti Sains Malaysia: rubber seed as food (IFRJ)

uses.note: only after thorough prolonged cooking — famine food
